story.title: Israeli Military Actions Challenge Trump's Gaza Peace Proposal
story.summary: Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu has rejected a recent peace proposal from U.S. President Donald Trump, which calls for the disarmament of Hamas and an Israeli withdrawal from Gaza. Netanyahu stated that the Israeli army will not retreat from its positions until Hamas is fully disarmed, contradicting the terms of a previous ceasefire agreement. Meanwhile, reports indicate that Trump would be disappointed if Israel does not accept the new plan.

explore_lenses.label: What changed on the ground?
explore_lenses.title: Israel is holding its current Gaza lines
explore_lenses.summary: Israel has publicly rejected the draft sequencing described by U.S. officials: Netanyahu says withdrawal will not begin before Hamas is completely disarmed, while the reported agreement envisages strikes stopping and a withdrawal beginning as disarmament proceeds.

claims.text: Netanyahu said on August 4 that Israel would not withdraw from its current positions in Gaza until Hamas had completely disarmed; he said the U.S. draft was not one Israel had agreed to.
The reported agreement calls for Hamas to begin disarming, Israel to halt strikes and begin withdrawing from the roughly 60% of Gaza that Israel controls.

Israel’s position is that verified, complete disarmament is a prerequisite for withdrawal; Hamas has characterized the arrangement as a package in which it needs confidence that Israel will carry out its obligations.

explore_lenses.label: How did the ceasefire reach this impasse?
explore_lenses.title: Phase two stalled over disarmament and withdrawal
explore_lenses.summary: The dispute centers on the unfinished second phase of the October 2025 ceasefire. The UN-endorsed framework links a staged Israeli withdrawal to Gaza’s demilitarization, an international stabilization force and a civilian Palestinian transition.

claims.text: The UN-endorsed plan says Israeli forces would progressively hand territory to an International Stabilization Force, with complete withdrawal tied to agreed demilitarization standards, milestones and timeframes; it also contemplates a residual security perimeter until Gaza is assessed as secure.
Nine months after the U.S.-brokered ceasefire was signed, negotiations had largely deadlocked over phase two, including Hamas disarmament and Gaza’s reconstruction.

UN officials have said the plan’s major elements are interdependent: Hamas and other armed groups’ disarmament, Israeli withdrawal, deployment of the stabilization force and enabling the National Committee for the Administration of Gaza to take transitional responsibilities.

Hamas’ stated condition is that disarmament belongs within a broader political package, including confidence that Israel will implement its side; Israel defines demilitarization broadly, extending from heavier weapons to tens of thousands of rifles.

explore_lenses.label: What steps are supposed to come next?
explore_lenses.title: A phased handover has no settled timetable
explore_lenses.summary: The proposed implementation path begins with limited police weapons transfers, then moves toward heavier-weapons decommissioning, tunnel destruction, international security deployment and a civilian administration. Israel’s public rejection of the draft makes those steps contingent rather than scheduled.

claims.text: The Board of Peace says its goal is complete weapons decommissioning and a shift to civilian governance; its Gaza representative met Netanyahu on August 3, and Hamas said it was awaiting a clear official response from the representative and mediators.

Forecast: U.S. and Board of Peace officials said Gaza police weapons could be transferred to the planned technocratic administration within two weeks, while heavy weapons, tunnels and other Hamas infrastructure could take 200 to 350 days to decommission.

The plan also anticipates an International Stabilization Force to secure aid routes, prevent weapons smuggling and train and vet Palestinian police; its operational mandate and deployment timeline remain incomplete.

Forecast: Board of Peace official Nickolay Mladenov said withdrawal must proceed “in lockstep” with decommissioning, indicating that withdrawal is expected to be phased rather than immediate if implementation resumes.

story_report.summary: Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu said on Aug. 4 that Israel would not leave its current positions in Gaza until Hamas had completely disarmed, saying the U.S. draft was not one Israel had accepted. The stance conflicts with a reported arrangement in which Hamas would begin disarming while Israel halted strikes and started withdrawing from territory it controls. The immediate consequence is a renewed impasse over whether disarmament must precede withdrawal or proceed alongside it.

sections.heading: Disarmament Sequencing Divides Israel and Hamas
sections.body: Israel’s position is that verified, complete disarmament must be achieved before any withdrawal. Hamas has described disarmament as part of a wider package and says it needs confidence that Israel will fulfill its own commitments. The disagreement extends to Israel’s definition of demilitarization, which encompasses heavier weapons as well as tens of thousands of rifles, while Hamas and Israeli officials differ over the sequence of reciprocal steps.

sections.heading: UN Plan Envisions Phased Gaza Transfer
sections.body: The UN-endorsed plan envisages Israeli forces progressively transferring territory to an International Stabilization Force, with complete withdrawal linked to agreed demilitarization standards, milestones and timeframes. It also allows for a residual Israeli security perimeter until Gaza is assessed as secure. UN officials have described disarmament, Israeli withdrawal, stabilization-force deployment and the transfer of transitional duties to a Gaza administrative committee as interdependent elements.

sections.heading: Implementation Depends on Security Arrangements
sections.body: The Board of Peace has said its objective is complete weapons decommissioning and civilian governance, while its Gaza representative met Netanyahu on Aug. 3. U.S. and Board officials forecast that police weapons could be transferred to a planned technocratic administration within two weeks, but that dismantling heavy weapons, tunnels and other Hamas infrastructure could require 200 to 350 days. Board official Nickolay Mladenov said withdrawal should proceed “in lockstep” with decommissioning.

unresolved.text: Public accounts do not establish a mutually accepted definition of complete disarmament, a verification authority or standard, or whether implementation requires strict sequencing rather than parallel measures.
No jointly accepted implementation text, withdrawal calendar or confirmed deployment date and operational mandate for the International Stabilization Force was publicly available as of Aug. 5, 2026.

related_stories.title: Progress Reported on Iran-Oman Deal to Reopen Strait of Hormuz
related_stories.summary: Officials from the US and Qatar have reported progress in negotiations between Iran and Oman regarding a deal to reopen the Strait of Hormuz. The emerging agreement would allow ships to enter the Persian Gulf through an Iranian-controlled route and exit via an Omani-controlled route, with service fees for security and environmental preservation. This development is seen as a potential breakthrough in efforts to stabilize the region.

related_stories.title: Russian Strikes on Kyiv Result in 17 Deaths Amid Air Defense Challenges
related_stories.summary: Overnight Russian missile and drone strikes on Kyiv have resulted in at least 17 fatalities and numerous injuries. Ukrainian officials reported that the attacks exploited the country's depleted air defenses, with no ballistic missiles successfully intercepted. President Zelenskyy has called for increased support from allies to bolster Ukraine's defense capabilities as the frequency and intensity of such assaults continue to rise.
